nodes.question: What are the common problems associated with Ru (II) complexes in light-harvesting applications?
nodes.answer: The common problems are the limited absorption of the (MLCT) band and the expensive expenditure on Ru (II) complexes.
nodes.paragraph: The limited absorption of (MLCT) band, in addition to the expensive expenditure on Ru (II) complexes, are common problems despite their increased efficiency [ 6]. The remarkable light-harvesting and durability properties associated with such photosensitizers can be ascribed to a process called (MLCT), which facilitates the rapid movement of photo - electric charges toward TiO2, exceeding electron recombina - tion using the oxidized dye component, rather than passing through the circuit [ 7, 8]. Moreover, metal-free organic sen - sitizers are preferred over Ru (II)-based sensitizers because of their numerous advantages, including versatile structure, economical manufacture, and enhanced molar extinction coefficients, which facilitate intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) between an electron-rich donor and an anchoring sec - tion via the use of a -spacer when light is absorbed [ 9, 10]. Co-sensitization is considered a promising technique for boosting the efficiency of DSSCs. The approach described above involves incorporating organic sensitizers (providing visible light) coupled with Ru (II) complexes (producing near-infrared light) to achieve extensive spectrum sensitiv - ity within the region of visible light and to enhance light absorption [ 11].

nodes.question: How do full-sun cocoa systems affect the age at which cocoa stops producing?
nodes.answer: Full-sun systems have been found to stop producing cocoa at a younger age compared to other systems.
nodes.paragraph: : (123456789) output in the long term is uncertain. Full-sun cocoa plantations can degrade soil fertility and biodiver - sity which impacts crop health and decreases resil- ience (Ariza-Salamanca et al. 2023; Tondoh et al. 2015; Bennett et al. 2021). Full-sun systems have also been found to stop producing cocoa at a younger age (Andres et al. 2016; Wessel and Quist-Wessel 2015). Agroforestry has therefore become a topic of interest as both a climate change mitigation measure through its retention of trees as well as an adaptation measure through regulation of micro-climates (e.g., shading cocoa from direct sunlight) and provision of diversi- fied income streams (Jagoret et al. 2019). With proper management, agroforestry systems can have 10 times the total system output (when non-cocoa harvests are included) compared to their full-sun counterparts, potentially contributing to greater food and income security (Niether et al. 2020; Jezeer et al. 2017).
